name: Schema 101 — quiz
abstract: Ten questions to check what you learned about schemas.
courseDescription: Notes, a deck, and a quiz about schemas and shared data rules that help systems work together.

grades.name: A
grades.message: Excellent. You can explain what a schema is and ask the right questions about one.

grades.name: B
grades.message: Strong work. Keep asking who owns the schema and how data is checked.

grades.name: C
grades.message: A sound start. Read the explanations, then check the notes for the ones you missed.

grades.name: D
grades.message: Go back to the key terms and the do’s and don’ts in the notes, then try again.

grades.name: F
grades.message: Start with the notes. Then take the quiz again.

questions.text: Why is a written schema useful to new staff and vendors?

options.text: It stores a copy of the data.
It replaces the need for training.
It documents the data so they can learn it fast.
It hides the data from them.

questions.hint: Think about learning the data quickly.
questions.explanation: Why it matters says a written schema documents your data, so new staff and vendors can learn it fast.

questions.text: Which problem can a schema help solve?

options.text: Systems run out of storage space.
Two systems use the same field name but mean different things.
Residents cannot find the County website.
Staff type data too slowly.

questions.hint: Think about field names and meanings.
questions.explanation: The Problem section says two systems can use the same field name and mean different things, so staff guess at meanings.

questions.text: Which step helps teams agree on what data means?

options.text: Let each vendor define fields in its own way.
Skip checking data to save time.
Change what a field means without telling users.
Define each field and its rules in a schema.

questions.hint: The solution starts with writing the plan down.
questions.explanation: The Solution section says to define each field and its rules in a schema and to name an owner.

options.text: A plan that describes the structure of data and the rules it follows.
A program that stores data.
A report about data quality.
A list of staff who can open the data.

questions.explanation: Key terms defines a schema as a plan that describes the structure of data: what it holds and the rules it follows.

questions.text: A constraint is a rule the data must follow, such as a required field.
questions.hint: Think about rules, such as a required field.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines a constraint as a rule the data must follow, such as a required field or a list of allowed values.

options.text: A County database for permits.
A tool that deletes old data.
A law about data privacy.
A shared vocabulary for data on web pages, built by an open community.

questions.hint: It is a vocabulary that many websites share.
questions.explanation: Key terms defines Schema.org as a shared vocabulary for data on web pages, built by an open community.

questions.text: A vendor says, “It works with anything.” What should you do?

options.text: Accept it, because the vendor knows best.
Ask the vendor to sign a longer contract.
Ask to see the vendor’s schema before you buy.
Wait until staff find a problem.

questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to ask to see a vendor’s schema before you buy, and not to accept “it works with anything” without proof.

questions.text: It is fine to change what a field means without telling anyone.
questions.hint: Think about the users of the data.
questions.explanation: Do’s and don’ts says to share every change to the schema with its users, and not to change what a field means without telling anyone.

questions.text: Which is a good question to ask about a schema?

options.text: Which font does the schema use?
Who owns it and decides what each field means?
Can we skip the schema this time?
How many pages is it?

questions.explanation: Questions to ask includes who owns the schema and decides what each field means.

questions.text: What should be true of a well-run schema?

options.text: One person owns it.
Each system uses a different name for the same fact.
It is kept secret from vendors.
Data is checked only after a problem.

questions.explanation: The Checklist includes “One person owns the schema.”
